metaphor.why: requests arrive like guests, the user store is the guest register, and login is the front desk

lens1.summary: FastAPI GET handler for /users/{user_id}. Builds a new Session and calls Session.login with the path parameter and a hard-coded password "pw", returning the login result.
inputs: user_id: str, taken directly from the URL path
lens1.outputs: Whatever Session.login returns (a boolean from the password comparison).
side_effects: Opens a SQLite connection through Session.__init__ -> UserRepo
Runs a database query through UserRepo.get
errors: Any sqlite3 error propagates as an HTTP 500
lens1.role: Entry point. Untrusted input enters here and flows into a SQL query two calls deeper.

lens2.text: This is the hotel's front door for one kind of visitor: someone asking about a specific guest by their room number. It sets up a fresh front-desk clerk and asks the clerk to check that guest in. The room number comes straight from the visitor, so whatever they say gets passed along.
lens2.example: If someone visits the address ending in /users/42, the clerk is asked to look up guest 42.
lens2.analogy: Like a door attendant who writes down whatever room number a stranger says and hands the note to the front desk without reading it.

lens3.text: This is the hotel's front door for one kind of visitor. It sets up a fresh front-desk clerk and asks the clerk to check that guest in. The room number comes straight from the visitor.

lens1.summary: Fetches the user record with self.users.get(user_id), then returns check_password(password, user).
errors: No handling for a missing user; get returns a cursor, not a row, so the comparison is against the wrong type
lens1.role: Middle step between the route and the data layer; forwards untrusted input to a SQL query.

lens2.text: The front-desk clerk looks the guest up in the register, then checks whether the password they gave matches what is on file.
lens2.example: A guest says they are number 42 with password 'pw'. The clerk finds the entry for 42 and compares.
lens2.analogy: Like a clerk flipping open the guest book and comparing a signature.

lens3.text: The front-desk clerk looks the guest up in the register, then checks whether the password they gave matches what is on file.

checks whether the password they gave matches

lens1.summary: Builds a SQL SELECT by %-formatting user_id into the string and runs it through BaseRepo.execute.
side_effects: Executes SQL against the connected database
errors: sqlite3.OperationalError on malformed SQL, which attacker input can trigger on purpose
lens1.role: Data-access leaf. The untrusted value from GET /users/{user_id} ends up inside the SQL text here.

lens2.text: This opens the guest register and finds a guest by number. It writes the request on a slip by copying the visitor's words straight into the middle of the instruction, then hands the slip to the records room.
lens2.example: If the visitor says their number is 42, the slip reads 'find guest 42'. If they say something sneaky, the slip says whatever they wrote.
lens2.analogy: Like a records room that follows any note it's handed, even if a stranger added extra lines to it.

lens3.text: This opens the guest register and finds a guest by number. It writes the request on a slip by copying the visitor's words into the instruction, then hands the slip to the records room.

pairs.plain: writes the request on a slip
copying the visitor's words into the instruction
hands the slip to the records room

findings.lens1: B608: user_id is interpolated into SQL text. It is reachable from GET /users/{user_id}, so a request can change the query, for example to return every row or to drop tables.
findings.lens2: A visitor can add their own instructions to the slip, and the records room will follow them.
findings.fix: Use a placeholder: self.conn.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", (user_id,)).

lens1.summary: Hashes the password with MD5 and compares the hex digest to the stored value.
inputs: user: stored hash (here, mistakenly a cursor)
errors: AttributeError if password is not a str

lens2.text: This scrambles the password the guest gave and checks it against the scrambled version on file. The scrambling method is old and fast, which makes it easy for someone with a copy of the file to guess passwords.
lens2.example: A guest says 'pw'. It is scrambled into a fixed code and compared with the code saved earlier.
lens2.analogy: Like protecting the guest book with a lock that has a well-known master key.

lens3.text: This scrambles the password the guest gave and checks it against the scrambled version on file. The scrambling method is old and fast.

pairs.plain: checks it against the scrambled version on file

pairs.technical: MD5 is unsuitable for password hashing

findings.lens1: B324: MD5 is a fast, broken hash. Stored MD5 password hashes can be cracked quickly with commodity GPUs.
findings.lens2: The lock on the guest book has a master key that many people already have.
findings.fix: Use a slow password hash such as Argon2id (argon2-cffi) or bcrypt, and compare with a constant-time check.

lens1.summary: POST /backup handler. Runs `tar` through the shell with the request's name concatenated into the command, then saves a record through a new UserRepo.
errors: Shell failures are ignored; subprocess.call's return code is not checked
lens1.role: Entry point. Untrusted input goes directly into a shell command.

lens2.text: This is the hotel's storage-room door. A visitor gives a name for a backup box, and the staff shouts an order to the storage room that includes the visitor's words, then notes the request in the register.
lens2.example: A visitor asks for a box called 'march'. The order becomes 'pack everything into march'.
lens2.analogy: Like a manager reading a guest's note aloud over the intercom to the whole staff without checking what it says.

lens3.text: A visitor gives a name for a backup box, and the staff shouts an order to the storage room that includes the visitor's words, then notes the request in the register.

pairs.plain: a name for a backup box
shouts an order to the storage room

pairs.technical: string concatenation into a shell command

pairs.plain: notes the request in the register

findings.lens1: B602: subprocess with shell=True and a request-controlled string. Reachable from POST /backup, so a request can run arbitrary commands on the server.
findings.lens2: A visitor can slip their own orders into the intercom message, and the staff will carry them out.
findings.fix: Pass an argument list without a shell: subprocess.run(["tar", "czf", f"{safe_name}.tgz", "data/"], check=True), after validating name against an allow-list pattern.

findings.lens1: LW-AUTH-MISSING (heuristic): POST /backup is called from the Admin page and changes server state, but no authentication dependency or check was found within three calls.
findings.lens2: Anyone who finds this address can ask the storage room to pack boxes. Nobody checks that they work at the hotel.
findings.fix: Require a logged-in admin: add a dependency such as current_user: CurrentAdmin = Depends(get_current_admin) to the route.

lens1.summary: React component that renders a 'Back up now' button. Its onClick handler `start` calls runBackup(name), which POSTs to /backup on the Python backend.
inputs: props.name: backup name typed into the Admin page's input
side_effects: On click: HTTP POST /backup through runBackup
errors: The returned promise is not awaited or caught, so a failed request is silent
lens1.role: UI trigger. A click here is the start of the path that reaches the server's shell command.

lens2.text: This is the button on the admin screen that says Back up now. When someone presses it, it sends the name from the text box to the hotel's back office and asks it to pack up the records.
lens2.example: Type nightly in the box, press the button, and the back office is asked to make a box called nightly.
lens2.analogy: Like a call bell at the front desk that rings the storage room with a note attached.

lens3.text: This is the button on the admin screen. When someone presses it, it sends the name from the text box to the back office.

pairs.plain: the button on the admin screen

lens1.summary: Sends an HTTP POST to /backup with JSON body {name} using axios. Lantern links this request to the Python handler shop.app.backup.
errors: Rejects on network errors or non-2xx responses
lens1.role: The frontend-to-backend hop: the name typed in the browser travels to backup(), which puts it into a shell command.

lens2.text: This is the messenger that carries the backup request from the screen to the back office. It hands over the name exactly as it was typed.
lens2.example: If the box says march, the messenger delivers a request to back up march.
lens2.analogy: Like a bellhop carrying a sealed note from the lobby to the storage room without reading it.
